utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Mahindaratne, I take it that it will be you who examines the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, I am ready, Mr. President. The Prosecution called Elisabeth Rehn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Usher, can you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will now be handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, you will first be examined by Ms. Mahindaratne who is counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Rehn.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: I'm Marta Elisabeth Rehn born in Finland.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you make a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, May I just intervene. I hate to ask the next question because it might not be considered not very polite, but we have different dates of birth for you on the statement. May I, nevertheless, ask you to indicate which year it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this is a quite a good start in the way that there is a sense of humour in this. They were so nice when interviewing me for the first time, they took away ten years of my age. So the correct one is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That answers my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, did you make a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 13th and 14th October 2005?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, thereafter, on the 21st February 2007, did you make a further statement clarifying and providing additional information to your previous statement, which you signed on 3rd April 2008?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, did you examine both these statements?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes, I did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document number 5315 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The Prosecution counsel is kindly requested to speak into the microphone, preferably the long microphone on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I hope that is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, in a moment, you will see on your screen a document, and if you could identify it as -- as your statement of 2005.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes. This is quite correct. This is -- this is the document we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, when you examined your statements, you provided two further changes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm again sorry to interrupt, but on our left screen, if we push the e-court button, I get a full blue screen. There we are. It apparently has been fixed. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Rehn, yesterday, when you examined your statements, you provided two further changes to your statement, and I'll -- so we don't waste much time, I will quickly read that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could take the statement to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You could follow the screen, Mrs. Rehn. Are you able to follow the screen?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You made a change to the first paragraph on page 3, the English version, where it is stated that you saw bodies of people killed and carcasses of animals. You corrected it by saying that you did not see bodies of people killed, and only carcasses of animals. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: This is totally correct, and the confusion is coming from the fact that when I gave my first interview in 2005, I told about a lot of things I had seen, not at least Kravica hill in Srebrenica with the bodies, and then there was a confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And then there was a further change you made, Mrs. Rehn, and that is --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could move, Mr. Registrar, to page 5 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, there, counting from top, in paragraph 7, that is the paragraph from the bottom, the one before the last paragraph. You refer to meeting President Tudjman on several occasions. You wished to correct it as two occasions: One in December 1995; and the second meeting was when you were the Special Rapporteur to the UN Secretary General. So these corrects were made yesterday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: That is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And subject to those changes, do you find -- did you find the contents of both your statements to be -- to accurately reflect what you stated to the members of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes. I went through these documents still yesterday evening, and there is nothing I could found that would not have been just in relation to what I have been telling.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And are the contents true, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Definitely, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you were asked the questions that you were asked of you by the members of the Office of the Prosecutor again today in court, would your responses be the same?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes. The contents will definitely be the same. Perhaps wordings can be a little bit different, but definitely the act, the meaning, and the contents are the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to tender --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Before that, if you could identify that -- you did identify that statement on the screen as your first statement?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there seems to be no objections, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P598.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P598 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could called number 5316, and that is the supplemental statement we just referred to, Mr. President, and if I could move that into evidence. Since it is a supplemental statement, Mr. President, it could be given perhaps a subnumber -- I'm sorry. That's not done here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, could you identify that this is the document on the screen is the supplemental statement that you made?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. There we even have the right date for my birth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to tender the statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that if the same questions were put as to the accuracy with which the second statement reflects what you said, whether it's in accordance with the truth, to the best of your knowledge, whether you would answer if the same questions would be put to you in the same way. Then there appear to be no objections against admission into evidence. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P599.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P599 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Rehn, when you provided the first statement, did you examine a number of documents, and did you provide explanations with regard to each of those documents in your first statement?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes. There were -- was a lot of reports and documents produced during time, those two and a half year as I functioned as the Special Rapporteur on the human rights situation in the territory of former Yugoslavia. So there were documents both regarding Croatia and all the other parts that I covered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And now, yesterday, did you have the opportunity to examine those -- those documents?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I went through them again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you satisfied that the contents of those documents were correct and your explanations provided in your first statement with regard to each of those documents was -- were accurate?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have tendered 17 documents under the 92 ter submission. I wish to withdraw one document which has already been tendered into evidence in a previous instance. May I move for the record, Mr. President, that is document number 17, the last document, which is also where I made an application to add it to the 65 ter list. That is an Secretary General's report, dated 21st December 1995, which has been tendered as P4777 already. With the exception of that, may I move that the other 16 documents be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection against any of the 16 documents? Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe we have tendered one of the other documents in the batch that we submitted last week, which is -- I think it's number 10 on the list, which is also 1D33-0336 and was tendered by the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Otherwise, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we are back from 17 now to 15. May I suggest that Mr. Registrar will put the 15 documents on a list and provisionally assign numbers to them, so that we'll then under those numbers admit them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with regard to the 15 documents, there is one document where I have requested Court -- made an application to add it to the 65 ter list. That is document on the 92 ter submission numbered 16. That is letter sent by United Nations High Commission for Human Rights To the president of the Republic of Croatia, dated 2nd October 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take that since there are no objections against admission into evidence, that there were no objections against adding this document to the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Registrar, you're invited to proceed as I suggested. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, for the record, may I also make an application that document number 4312, that is the 65 ter number, be admitted under seal. I could -- if an explanation is required, I could explain in private sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection against this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what document we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Those are the minutes of the meeting between the witness and members of the Croatian government and international bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the 9th of October, 1995, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we go briefly into private session, so you can explain what reason that might have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I read the summary of the witness's 92 ter submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you have explained to Mrs. Rehn what the summary is for.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ms. Elisabeth Rehn was the United Nations Special Rapporteur of the Commission on Human Rights for the situation on the territory of former Yugoslavia from September 1995 to January 1998. In this capacity, she visited the Krajina following Operation Storm. She conducted meetings with members of the Croatian government, including the president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman; the Minister of Defence, Gojko Susak; and the Minister of the Interior, Ivan Jarnjak, where crimes committed by members of the Croatian forces and the potential for the Serb population to return to the region were discussed. She inquired from representatives of the government of the Republic of Croatia regarding measures taken to prevent and investigate crimes and received their responses. Mrs. Rehn reported her findings to, inter alia, the United Nations General Assembly and the United Nations Security Council. Mrs. Rehn was a member of the parliament of Finland from 1979 to 1995, the minister of Defence from 1990 to 1995, and presidential candidate in 1994 and 2000. In January 1998, she was appointed to the United Nations Special Representative -- I'm sorry. She was appointed as the United Nation's Special Representative to the Secretary-General in Bosnia and Herzegovina and held that appointment until 1999. That concludes the summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document number 309, please. Mr. President, may I request that I be permitted to give -- allow the witness to go through hard copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems very practical.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, if you wish to go through the hard copies, it's at tab 3 of your binder. The tabs are marked. Now, when you compiled reports, Mrs. Rehn, on situation in Croatia, you received responses from the -- the Croatian government. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And is this document such a response submitted to you by the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P600.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P600 is admitted into evidence. Ms. Mahindaratne, I see that on your witness P141 list, you refer to witness statement P141, which could create some confusion since P141 looks as if it was an exhibit number, although it's clear that you did not intend this to be an exhibit number. If you would make that Prosecution witness or even the name of the witness, since there are no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will do that, Mr. President. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document 4351, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Rehn, first, I'd like to look at -- I'd like to you look at your statement while the document is being brought up on the screen, and your statement is at tab 1. Could you follow it. In page 5 of your statement, if I could take to you paragraph 5 -- I'm sorry, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And from that point up to page 6, paragraph 5, you referred to a meeting you had with President Tudjman, Mr. Jarnjak, and Minister Susak. Now, the document I'd like you to look at are the minutes. It's on the screen. If you wish to look at the hard copy, it's at tab number 3 -- I'm sorry, tab number 11 of your binder. Are these the minutes containing a report of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, who compiled these minutes?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: You can see on the screen or I can see or everybody can see that I had with me on the meetings Roman Werocevski [phoen] from the Centre for Human Rights Representing the commission that always follow me; and then for the Croatian human rights office, Diakite Mamadi, and he was the one, Mr. Mamadi, who always made the minutes when he was travelling with us. So these minutes are made by him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you meet these individuals, the president and the minister, at one meeting or in separate meetings?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: It was always separate meetings. It's the best way you're doing it, also the practical way, because it is really difficult to get presidents and ministers together at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could move to the next page -- I'm sorry. It's a page after that, page number 3. That is the ERN 77. That's correct. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, I'd like, Mrs. Rehn, if you could focus on paragraph number 10. Now this is -- this refers to your meeting with Mr. Jarnjak.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Oh, oh, oh, oh.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the document on the screen. If you could just look at paragraph number 10, there is a discussion about illegal and forcible evictions from military apartments. And under paragraph number 10, the third paragraph it reads like this: "Asked about the obligation of the Ministry of Interior and especially why the civilian police cannot prevent violence and assaults committed in this matter, Minister Jarnjak mentioned that the civilian police have always been present and did everything within their authority and competence. He mentioned that in forcible evictions, judicial sanctions are required. However, if the perpetrators are military men, only the military police is competent and they do not have any authority to intervene." Now, do you recall that statement being made by Mr. Jarnjak?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, that same day, you met the Minister of Defence, Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could move down to the page with ERN number 7185. I know it's difficult to go by the ERN number. It's just that the page numbering is a little messed up. If we could go to the top of the document, you could follow that. Yes. That page, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, from this page onwards, you have the minutes of your meeting with Mr. Susak. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes. He didn't like me at all, and my reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did he inform you as to why he did not like your reports?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Hmm. It was because of that he thought that we have been too much focussing on the military approach instead of looking into all the criminal acts that had been done by civilians, and also what has happened before my time as Special Rapporteur.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now if we could move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, there, under paragraph 7, it seems that the same issue, that of illegal eviction from military apartments, has been discussed with Mr. Susak. Now, was his response on this issue consistent with what Mr. Jarnjak told you; that is, that only the military police could be utilized to resolve this situation, or was it contradictory?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: It was contradictory in the sense that Minister Jarnjak made it clear that the civilian police cannot interfere when it is a military eviction; but, again, according to Minister Susak, he made it quite clear that there must be a court order that they cannot force anyone to leave. And, so, they need a special request from the court, and the courts are responsible to deal with all complaints. But then --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, do you recall if, in fact, Mr. Susak confirmed that civilian police could not intervene at this stage, or if he, in fact -- did he address that at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have never done this before, but the relevance of this line of question escapes me on evictions for military personnel in November of 1995, so if we could get at least a proffer as to what the relevance of this inquiry is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, The relevance is that we have had led a lot of evidence here about the ability of the civilian police to interfere with the military when certain acts of violence are committed, you know. It is -- if you go back it Mr. Jarnjak's minutes regarding Mr. Jarnjak's discussion, the reference is to violence and it is not just eviction. The reference is to violence perpetrated by military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then I have a standing objection to this. This requires going into Croatian law on who owns the military apartments. There is an entire procedure. As a matter of fact, it is in the documents she has tendered, a responses from the Croatian government outlining all of the laws, which is completely different than a security situation generally in a territory, which is what was discussed previously. But she can use her time as she wishes, but we have a standing objection to the relevance of who has ownership to military apartments and who is responsible under the law for conducting an eviction from a military apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't wish to waste time since I have finish this. I will make arguments. The document is before the Chamber. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, let me take you to your -- the minutes of your meeting with Mr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that is, if could you go back, Mr. Registrar, to page bearing ERN number 7183.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Rehn, you have described this meeting and your conversation with Mr. Tudjman already in your statement. Do you confirm that this -- these are the minutes of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could go to the next page, I'd like to draw your attention, Mrs. Rehn, to the paragraph numbered 6 where it is states, noted that: "The Special Rapporteur commented that a peaceful solution is most important even if there is so much hatred and distrust among people. Therefore, the protection of all human rights of Serbs should be guaranteed, and justice is a basic human rights. A fair trial should be guaranteed and justice made without delay for those who have been accused for looting and arson, to demonstrate that the judiciary is functioning. She mentioned the situation in Kuplensko camp, inquiring whether the return of all refugees would take some time." And then there is a discussion between you and Mr. Tudjman. And then under paragraph numbered 7, the second paragraph, Mr. Tudjman goes on addressing you: "He pointed out the goodwill of Croatia by referring to a possible decree on amnesty (which already created some resistance) that trials will be initiated for those accused only for war crimes and not armed rebellion. According to the president, this decision is not a positive step towards normalization of..." -- Is, I'm sorry. "According to the president, this decision is a positive step towards the normalization of relations between Croatia and Serbia." Now, Mrs. Rehn, you, yourself, in some of your reports call for a general amnesty for the former members of the combatants of the so-called RSK. Now, could you explain when the international community asked for a general amnesty, as it is also stated here, what exactly were you asking for? Was it amnesty against prosecution of crimes, or amnesty --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is leading the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. I haven't finished my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the leading part is there already apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could please rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Well, Mrs. Rehn, could you explain to Court what that amnesty was, the general amnesty that the international community was calling for?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: It is quite clear that the international community was definitely not asking for an amnesty for criminals, for criminal acts and war crimes even, but what we asked for was an amnesty so that people whoever side they represented were not afraid of returning back home again. That was especially important in the Croatian -- of the Serbs who been leaving the -- the Krajina region, and that they are not afraid of being -- being just taken in prison when they are returning back home again, if they can return back home. And this is what was meant by the whole international community. We discussed it a lot, that an amnesty is important. But if you only point out those names they were some hundreds who had got amnesty, then it is creating a fear with the others that, "If I'm not on that list, what will happen to me," even if they were ordinary combatants obeying orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at your meeting with Mr. Tudjman, he says that an amnesty was being considered for those -- for -- and it says: Trials will be initiated for those accused only for war crimes and not armed rebellion." So did you understand Mr. Tudjman to be speaking of that same type of amnesty that the international community was referring to?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. I think that he had a very good intention in this; but when you look then what it will lead to and the fears that people had, it was not in that sense the correct way of doing this. So, therefore, we warned about this and the international community asked for the general amnesty; of course, excluding criminals.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P601.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P601 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just want -- wish to point out that document is, in fact, included in the 92 ter submission, Mr. Register, so that there won't be any duplicity in assigning numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar, the list is back to 14. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document 4365, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, if you wish to look at the hard copy, it's at tab 12. Now, in your statement, you refer to sending a letter to the foreign minister of Croatia, inquiring about the -- an investigation into the incident that occurred in Grubori on 25th August 1995. Now, if you could look at the document which is on the screen or the hard copies, this is a document, a letter that you sent?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if I could -- if we could go to page 2 of the English -- English document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, if I could just take your attention to paragraph 3, on the first page of the letter, you write: "With regard to the reported investigation of the Grubori case, it is mentioned in the recent report by the government of the Republic of Croatia on the implementation of Security Council Resolution 1019, 1995, that the site of the crime was inspected by police on the same day on which it was reported by the UN Human Rights Action Team on 25 August 1995,(page 8). "Furthermore, General Cermak stated in an interview with UN personnel on 26 August, that the Croatian authorities reached the village and took care of the people on the evening of 25th August. He also remarked in a letter to the UN, dated 31 August, that he personally visited the hamlet the following day." Now what was the basis of that information? From where did you gather that information?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: This was the information I got from my own staff, the United Nations Human Rights staff visiting the place and others within UNCRO. So it was discussions, it was reports that were given, and personal visits by those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And who informed you about the statement Mr. Cermak had made about this matter?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: That is something I definitely can't remember who was the person, because, as you know, a Special Rapporteur is working with a team of people who are telling what has happened there, what they have followed up; and then we are making the conclusions out of this. And, unfortunately, I don't have that, that information, who exactly was the person in our team.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could take you to the next page, Mrs. Rehn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could move to page 2, both B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There, under the paragraph numbered 2, there's a list of registration numbers of vehicles, as being vehicles that were observed in the vicinity of Grubori on 25th August 1995. Now, from where did you get those numbers?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: It is exactly the same, that the UN team of -- from the UNCRO and our people, the human rights office people, had been watching this. They were present there, and they collectively told this during an information meeting to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you ever receive a response from the Croatian government identifying to whom those vehicles belonged to at the time or who used those vehicles? Did you get a response to this inquiry?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I got a lot of answering letters to different cases, and I'm very grateful for the way that the Croatian government acted in this. But this specific case was something I never could get more than around that. Investigations are still going on. And that was, of course, a little bit worrying with regard to the fact that they could give exact dates like the register numbers of the vehicles and at which hour what happened; and so on, not to mention the very -- very odd UN meeting that are being called for, so that every person from Grubori almost was away from -- from the village. I not only requested from Minister Granic about this, but also from his staff that I met now and then, and nobody could give me a relevant answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Rehn, to your knowledge, during your tenure as Special Rapporteur, are you aware that your office or any party ever received a satisfactory response from the Croatian government or the Croatian authorities about an investigation into the Grubori incident?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not. They didn't receive because that was an ongoing story. One could, of course, ask that why just one very sad incident when there were so many, but my method of working was that the individuals, the human rights or the individuals, were the most important. So even one single case should have a proper answer, and we never got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move to tendered this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there appear to be any objections, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P602.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P602 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I call up document 2566, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, that document is not in your tab. You will probably see it on the screen in a moment?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the document we just looked at, you -- in that first paragraph I read out to you, it was stated that Mr. Cermak had remarked in a letter to the UN, dated 31st August, that he personally visited the hamlet the following day. Now, are you -- have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You refer to a letter written by Mr. Cermak to the UN regarding his visit to the Grubori area the following day. At the time, was a copy of that letter shown to you, or did anybody inform that you such a letter was written?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: It was informed that there was a letter. Of course, I can't -- if I'm just sticking to the truth, I can't remember that it would have been shown to me. But at least I never got a copy, and I can't recall that I would have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in this document, Mr. Cermak describes -- provides a report of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could move the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the last paragraph, Mr. Cermak reports as this: "I personally visited the area the following day and convinced myself of the truthfulness and the course of the incidents in question." And I just want to point that out because that is what you had reported in your letter to the minister of foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may of move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I hear of no objections, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P603.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P603 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document number 5317, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, while the document is coming up, Mrs. Rehn, if I could just take to you your statement, the 2005 statement. At page 8, paragraph 5 you refer to two letters, where you say: "In the Secretary-General's report ER/2, paragraph 28, there is an reference to letters written by the high commissioner for human rights to President Tudjman with respect to the return of the Serbs being prevented by serious violations of human rights together with executive and legislative measures. I am familiar with both those letters, and I produce a copy of the letter dated 18 August 1995. Now, the other letter was not available at the time. Do you recognise document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that the other letter, dated 2nd October 1995, that you referred to in this paragraph --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender this document into evidence, and it is part of the 92 ter submission. At the end of the day's sessions, I will inform Mr. Registrar as to what documents were tendered through the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because it reduces the size of the list to 13 now. I wonder whether we ever come to zero. Any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour. I just want to the note for the record that I need those numbers, so that I can conduct the cross-examination and refer back to them. We'll figure out during the break how I'm going to refer to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As always, the breaks are more busy than what happens this Court. Mr. Registrar, do you think the list, which is now reduced to 13, could be produced after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours, and this exhibit becomes P604.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P604 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes examination-in-chief, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Having the numbers only after that break, would that cause you major problems at this moment, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It won't be a major problem if I could just get the Court's indulgence if I fumble around a bit trying to find the right document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will show the same patience as we usually do. Whether that is patient enough is still to be seen. Mrs. Rehn, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, good morning.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would like to start by taking you to the 4 December 1995 meeting that you had with President Tudjman which is, I believe, at page 5 of your first statement. And you, in your statement, make several characterizations about President Tudjman during that meeting. You say, in your statement: "I remember telling Tudjman that the perpetrators of crimes ..." -- I'm sorry. It starts above that. "My impression of President Tudjman when I spoke to him on more than one occasion was that he was quite detached whenever we tried to speak about the Serbian refugees returning to the Krajina. He was not interested in that particular subject. In the minutes, it was recorded and I remember that Tudjman suggested that to punish the perpetrators of crimes in Operation Storm would cause problems, and he was clearly not interested in punishing anyone. He indicated that in the main the perpetrators were civilians and made no reference to crimes being committed by the military. In effect, he was trying to protect the good name of the Croatian army." And then the last paragraph is: "I remember telling Tudjman that the perpetrators of crimes, like looting and arson, should be dealt with quickly to show the judicial system was working. Tudjman responded by talking about the crimes that were committed by the Muslims on the Croats. In effect, he was not interested in what I was saying. He was on the one hand trying to justify what had happened by talking about crimes committed against Croats elsewhere or during another time, and I clearly got the impression after talking to him on several occasions that there was no political will to punish the perpetrators of crimes committed during Operation Storm."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I point out that there was an amendment to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was about to do that, Your Honour. I was just waiting for the translation to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you are -- yes. Now your comment appears on screen. I was listening to the French channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to make -- I just waiting for the translation to finish, and then I was going to point that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Rehn, you have already point out for us this morning that where in the statement it says you spoke to him on several occasions, that's actually two occasions?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And it is fair to say that these impressions were then formed from that meeting on the 4th of December, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: It was quite a long meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, we have the audiotape. I don't know if you're aware that President Tudjman taped all his conversations. We are going to play for you - I believe it is a 22 minute meeting - the entire meeting, and I'd ask to you listen closely and try to note in as you listen where you made or where these impressions were formed. And you'll see a transcript also as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could have that, Mr. Registrar. I also have a transcript in hard copy for the witness, so that she can make notations or refer to the specific portions of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then after we're done, I will take you back to your statement and ask you to identify where in the conversations you believe President Tudjman made such assertions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can I also ask if there is a copy available of the transcript for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In e-court. I have it call it up. I'm sorry. It is 1D40-0087.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Yes. The day before yesterday, very late in the evening, after a very interesting, very useful tour around the territory of the former Yugoslavia, so I have learned a lot. Everything is not nice, what I have learned, unfortunately. But I have been very well received all over, and I believe that the atmosphere is getting very open now." "You had discussions with my people in Croatian already?" "I have had with just internal affairs with social welfare, and I am very pleased that there is a possibility to meet with my former colleague, Defence Minister Susak, on the airport, because I'm leaving directly from here to Rome to start with and then back home." "Have you been already in Sarajevo or Belgrade?" "I was -- I was last time. Now my tour was really going to Banja Luka to Pristina to Mostar; and, yesterday, I went to East Slavonia, Sector East, and that's something that I had find very important, that the -- hopefully good agreement can be fulfilled to all its parts."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Dear Madam, as you stated, unfortunately some things could not be done. But you must keep in mind that the things that happened in the years during the dissolution of Yugoslavia during the Yugoslav Communist Serb aggression and everything that happened up until these agreements, first the Washington Agreement, the Croatian Muslim agreement, and the Dayton now, that this was one of the most complicated world crisis, and that it is important that we get out of this crisis in order to be able to truly dedicate ourselves to humanitarian issues and to the removal of all factors which caused people to suffer, which caused people from those areas, and in general which caused such an abnormal suffering. "Now we are after all on the road to that after the Dayton Accords and hopefully after the signing in Paris towards the normalisation of our relations which will enable us to deal with these issues that you and your delegation are focussing on." "You have not been able to see nice things during your visit. However, it should be borne in mind that what has happened in the years after the dissolution of Yugoslavia with the Yugo-Communist Serb aggression and everything after, first of all, the Washington Agreements between the Croats and the Muslims in Bosnia, and now recently the Dayton Agreements, does represent one of the most complicated local crisis. What is essential now is to leave this crisis behind to resolve it, so that we can devote ourselves to humanitarian issues, to the elimination of everything that has caused so much suffering for all the people in the region, to get out, out of this abnormal, truly abnormal situation. Nevertheless, now, after the Dayton Agreements and hopefully after the signing of all of documents in Paris, we will be on the way towards normalisation, and then we can devote ourselves fully to the issues which are your concern." "Mr. President, I am very much supporting your thoughts in this, because I have been all the time stating that I hope that in my work, I can come more away from just bookkeeping on events that, it should be more a question of conclusions of recommendations of how we can face the future and just work together for better understanding of human rights, instead of just telling that those were murdered there, those were looted, those were -- their houses were burnt up, and they are in mass graves. We should come over this situation."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is precisely the thought that I wanted to express myself. We in Croatia wanted to avoid everything that took place, and we propose that after Tito, this Yugoslav crisis by peaceful means on a confederal basis. We were faced with everything that we were; therefore, Croatia and then Bosnia suffered such an aggression I don't know if you visited Vukovar or not, but a third of Croatia was destroyed. Four hundred thousand Croats, Hungarians, Czechs, Slovaks, were forced out of their homes, and naturally people were murders. It is it understand that in the course of the liberation of these areas, on the Croatian side it was also impossible to constrain the fighting to fighting in gloves. Therefore, first of all, the Yugo-Communist army and the Serbs committed terrible crimes in such an aggression aimed at creating Greater Serbia. And later in the liberation of these areas, it was also impossible to prevent people who had suffered and who were now returning to those areas from committing acts of revenge and stupidity such as destroying homes and so forth. Therefore, it is more important now to forget all of this as soon as possible and to build normal relations among people, among nations; rather, even though it is necessary to punish individuals for war crimes, if we went to this breadth, if we were to approach this issue so broadly, this would mean a new deepening of mistrust and conflict. So it is more important that we develop a new order and establish trust." [Previous translation continues] ... "which I also wanted to express. We in Croatian also wanted to avoid such developments; and after Tito, we wanted to propose. We proposed a solution of the crisis by peaceful means on a confederal basis. However, later on, we were faced with everything that we suffered in Croatian. And later on in Bosnia, we suffered such a terrible aggression. I don't know whether you have been to Vukovar or not." "Oh, yes. I was yesterday. I could see in my own eyes." "One third of Croatian was destroyed. More than 400.000 people were expelled, Croats, Hungarians, Czechs, Slovaks; and many of them also lost their lives. And in the process of liberation in these areas by Croatian forces, one couldn't remain just at war. War is not conduct in the gloves anywhere in the world. First of all, it was the Yugoslav Communist and the Serbian aggression which was the cause of horrendous crimes in the area. In their aggression, their aim is to create a Greater Serbia. Later on, during the liberation, of course we couldn't fully restrain our people. There were many people there who suffered loss of human life, loss of their relatives, sacrifices, loss of property, and so forth. Some of them resort to acts of revenge, I mean to stupid things such as destruction of homes and so forth." "So stupid." "What is important, however, is to forget all this, and turn to normalisation of relations among people, among nations in the region. The -- certain individuals, of course, have to be punished for the acts they have committed. But if we go too broadly in this respect, I think this would only deepen the distrust and possibly lead to new conflicts. So what is important I believe that we should turn our attention fully to the establishment of a new order in the region." "Yes. I believe that it's important really to not the look too much in what has been going on. Of course, it is very difficult to forget when you have lost all what you are believing in, to your love, to your relatives, your home, and even your homeland. But perhaps we should more look at not at the revenge, more at the justice and the truth, because there is always a time when the truth is coming -- coming true, and the sooner the better. I have been especially concerned during this tour with just questions of all the return of refugees. With the missing people, that seems to be a very difficult question because that is something that every person wants to know what happened. Even if you have the message that he is killed or she is killed, it's better than not to know. And then, of course, just even the mental health of the children, because you have the future, that's very important. So there have been many things that I have been concerned about, and sometimes I have had the feeling that perhaps there is not the real understanding well in words, but perhaps not in action. And I'm now not talking about Croatia, I'm talking for the whole territory. Because if we are going to implement the agreement from Dayton, there must be the respect for these rights. You know, Mr. President, that I'm a member of the European Parliament, and for us it is industrial important that Croatia who has been in some way in the lead, though, in the democratic procedure for this -- left from the former Yugoslavia, that you can implement as soon as possible the normal democracy and justice, human rights."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Rest assured that Croatian authorities are absolutely focussed in that sense. You see, consenting to the Dayton Accords, which means consenting it a peaceful solution concerning the liberation of the occupied territories of Eastern Slavonia, was -- was received with great dissatisfaction by a significant number of the Croatian public, who were saying "Why did we proceed to liberate Eastern Slavonia with military forces as we had done in the case of Western Slavonia, Knin, and so on," because such a huge amount of hatred and distrust have accumulated. But assessing that peace was of a greater importance, and we didn't want all the Serbs to leave. We wanted to establish relations based on trust, and based on our experiences in Knin where we also didn't want all the Serbs to leave. Therefore, the Croatian government will truly attempt to act within the framework of a peaceful solution in the liberated territories, guaranteeing civil rights, and especially resolving issues regarding missing persons which is painful and which is accepted with great difficulty by the people even when they know that the victims are dead..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I did not hear French translation on channel 5 of the last portion of the recorded interview. I'm just wondering how to proceed because I'm switching from one channel to another, and I do not exactly where it started. I suggest that, at this moment, we continue to hear the recording, and that during the break, we'll verify to what extent the French translation is provided. Then how to resolve that is another matter because I would not like to play the whole of the 20 minutes again. Let's proceed and I'll listen to the French translation for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] " ...who have great difficulty to come to terms with this situation. And when it comes to concessions, as far as the Croatian side is concerned, we have also contributed. We have given concessions because there can be no peace without concessions provided by all sides. Therefore, we have the dissatisfaction of those people who due to the evil they had suffered want to proceed with military combat operations and commit acts of revenge. But on a whole, in Croatia, we have such a stable democratic order that is necessary in order to ensure the development of the principles along the lines you had mentioned earlier." [Previous translation continues] ... "Croatian authorities, Croatian government is absolutely [indiscernible] and commited with this respect. We have agreed to the Dayton Agreement, that is, to the peaceful solution concerning the liberation of the remaining occupied parts of the Republic of Croatia that is Eastern Slavonia. This has even caused certain discontent among a number of the Croatian people and Croatian public because some people are saying, 'Why didn't we go and solve the issue militarily as we did with Western Slavonia, with Knin, and so forth,' because so much hatred and so must distrust has accumulated over the recent period. However, we are fully aware of the fact that peace is more important. We certainly do not want and have not wanted all the Serbs to leave, and we didn't want -- we offer them the protection of human rights and so forth, in our attempts to peacefully liberate all our areas. And we have also, on a number of times, at a number of times, guaranteed all human rights to them. Then, of course, there is particular the issue, the painful issue of missing persons, which is something that many people find difficult to accept, and even when they know that their friend, relatives, members of their families are dead. But still thousands of people find it difficult to reconcile themselves with such a state of affairs and who also find it difficult to recognise themselves with the concessions. I mean, Croatia has also made its contributions in this regard. We have made concessions because there is no peace without concessions on all the parties involved. And, hence, the dissatisfaction of the part of the people who have suffered so much over the past period, and this is why they want to see the matters solved militarily and even feel feelings of revenge. But, nevertheless, we have a stable democratic order, and you can rest assured that we shall provide for the implementation of all the principles in our [indiscernible]."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Almost 20 years ago, I wrote about the need to Scandinavise this area, both in the sense of democratisation and mutual recognition and co-existence of different ethnicities. In the top echelons of Croatian authorities, I believe there are numerous humanists, according to their calling, their profession, their personal sentiments. The president of the parliament is a writer; the deputy prime minister, a lady, is also a humanist here. We have one of my closest associates, also a writer, a humanist, and so on. In Croatia, in this democratic government, there are truly not only people of -- who have generally a political commitment. There are people who are truly supportive when it comes to Croatia and committed towards Croatia's contribution and Bosnia and Herzegovina, on a whole, towards the normalization of the Croatian-Muslim, the Croatian-Serb relations, and, as I said, this area, instead of being a keg of gunpowder, should become, in accordance with the example of Scandinavia, an area of peace and cooperation amongst nations." [Previous translation continues] ... wrote about the need and necessity to Scandinavise this area, as I called it, on the basis of democratization and mutual recognition and co-existence among peoples and nations. I believe that at the very top of Croatian government there are more humanists by profession and by feeling. The Speaker of our parliament, our vice-premier present here, one of my first associates is also a man of letters and a humanist, so in the Croatian democratic government, we don't have only a general political commitment to the those principles but also their composition goes to show that there are people who truly committed, so that Croatia -- not only in Croatia itself but also in Bosnia and Herzegovina can contribute to the overall normalization of the relations between the Croats and the Muslims, between the Croats and the Serbs, so that this area does not become what it has been in the past, as they call it, a gunpowder keg but, rather, an example, along the example of Scandinavian countries of peace and cooperation among peoples." "Yes, I'm very pleased to be listening to this. There is quite a lot of Nordic mafia present here just now, with Stoltenberg and Bildt and Rehn and so on, but I hope that this will really be something that is positive and not negative in, in any case, because we really want to do, do our best. I think that just in this democracy process ... that those who now are accused for -- for the looting and killing and so on during Operation Storm, or the Serbian side, there are quite a lot of them in prison that, if possible, even I -- if I know it is a very difficult process, because no courts are capable of being very, very -- just short in time with cases like this, when there are huge amount of them, but it should be good if they could be dealt with quite quickly. So there is the feeling that this is something where the justice is working and they will have then a fair trial. Of course it will be fair, but the trial is also fair when it comes quite, quite soon after committing the crimes. And something I'm also concerned about this, perhaps the situation with the camps, just like Velika Kladusa region, I believe they have difficulties, if there is possible to improvements with their living, because it takes time before they are returning, one by one of course, but so that should be quite important."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "You see, with regards to refugees from Velika Kladusa, this is a good illustration of how complex the situation here is because the Muslims are afraid to return among the Muslim population. And in this case we, Croatia, have done everything we could, our utmost. We even called upon the president and the Turkish government to exert their influence on the Muslim leadership, and we also sent a unit of Croatian police in order to enable them to return as soon as possible. Well, the example of the refugees from Velika Kladusa, also goes to show how complex the situation is, because this is a case of Muslims being afraid to come back among Muslims ..." -- "Their own."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "And we, the Republic of Croatia, have done everything. We have also asked the Turkish government to help us so that they bring their influence to bear on the Muslim leadership. Even to send a police unit. And we have also sent a unit of the Croatian police there so that this matter can be dealt with as soon as possible. As for the first issue you raised, I must say, frankly, that I had already passed a decision on abolition of those who had participated in the rebellion, the Serbs who had participated in the rebellion against Croatian authorities, except for war criminals. I must admit that we are encountering resistance from a formally legal perspective, including our judiciary, and recently I said, Do not put people on trial only because they participated in the armed rebellion because, in a way, they were forced to do that. Try people only if they had committed war crimes. Therefore, we, in Croatia, shall truly attempt to take action along the lines which you described, that we need to let people out of the jails as soon as possible because this is an important step towards establishing and renewing mutual trust between the Croats and Serbs in Croatia and also the normalization of the Croat-Serb relations as a whole." [Previous translation continues] ... "speaking, I have already issued a decision, a decree on abolition for all the Serbs who took part in the rebellion against Croatian authorities, against the Croatian government, excepting war criminals, of course. I must say that we do meet with certain resistance in formal legal terms, even from the courts, but even recently I said, Don't try those people who took part in the rebellion because they were forced to. Just try those who are guilty of war crimes, and we shall really do everything operated on such levels. And I also said, 'Release all those people who are not guilty of war crimes, release them from prison.' We believe that this is an important step towards the rebuilding of trust between the Croats and the Serbs in Croatia and, of course, within the scope of all or normalization of relations between Croatia and Serbia."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "And we are doing this despite the fact that there those are who are apposed to us, who are radical and extremist element, who are criticizing us, and saying 'Why negotiate, why reconcile with those who had committed the aggression?' But we shall persevere. [Previous translation continues] ..."although they are in the opposition ranks, in radical extremist ranks, there are criticisms, 'Why negotiate with these people, why come to terms with them, since they are taken part in the aggression?' But, nevertheless, we shall persevere along the lines which I mentioned." "Yes. I believe it is very important for all of us. As you know, Europe has put some conditions for construction, budget lines, and so on. And for us it is very important that sooner or later, there should be a former Yugoslavia who totally is a part of the European Union Council to start with, and I have the feeling that you are the ones to be starting this process. So my role is, of course, very much of a Rapporteur, but I'm not very, very happy to only report, as I told you in the beginning. I should very much like to contribute to the democratic process in the whole territory; and, therefore, you can certainly count on me. Of course, I'm going to report badly things -- bad things if there are nasty things to report on. I hope that I will be unnecessary soon, but I'm not so far, unfortunately."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The situation that we are in, we have to try to leave it as so as possible." [Previous translation continues] ... "need to strive to get out of the situation in which we find ours, we have to try to leave it as soon as possible." "Yes. We have our national day the day after tomorrow. Can I bring your regards, Mr. President, to my president?" "My people [indiscernible]." "I hope so."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was going to suggest for the interpreters that we take an earlier break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a breath first, and then a break as well. Then we also could try to verify what is there as far as French translation is concerned, also keeping in mind that, of course, we heard most of what was spoken in B/C/S twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would also give an opportunity to Mrs. Rehn perhaps to go through the transcript and to prepare for the answer to the question you put to her before playing this audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I could just ask her just to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The three voices we hear on the audio are your voice, President Tudjman's voice, and President Tudjman's interpreter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: That was totally correct, and it was quite interesting to memorize again that discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we take a break firsts. We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late start. It will not be of much consolation to you if I add that it was for good reasons, but it was. Then before we continue, looking at the transcript, Mrs. Rehn, in relation to your second statement, I asked you in a bit of a summarized form whether it accurately reflect what happened you said, whether you would give the same answers, and the transcript doesn't give any explicit confirmation of that, but I understood that you confirmed that it was the same with the second as with the first one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now it is on the transcript. Then, yes, are you ready to continue, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, would you agree with me that one of the -- President Tudjman's points in your meeting of the 4th of December was to emphasise his desire for reconciliation between Serbs and Croats both within Croatia and the generally the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: That is absolutely true and that is also mentioned by me in my reports. You could well follow in our discussion, of course, the diplomatic language that is always made in a certain way when a president and a former minister is present, but it's absolutely true that he was looking for a reconciliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And having heard the audiotape, do you believe that -- or would you agree that in the context of that discussion about reconciliation, President Tudjman spoke of the need to amnesty people who -- except for people who had committed war crimes?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes. This exception is very important. It was quite clear also repeated by me, that the amnesty was meant for those who had not committed war crimes or real crimes. They can be civilian crimes, too. But what perhaps was missing from the discussion was the question I put about the lootings and misbehaviour from the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We will get to, in a little while, the issue of whether civilian crimes were covered by the general amnesty and whether the international community wanted them covered by the general amnesty. But for our purposes here, to go back to your statement, for example, you say, at page 5 of your statement: "I remember telling Tudjman that the perpetrators of crimes like looting and arson should be dealt with quickly to show the judicial system was working. Tudjman responded by talking about the crimes that were committed by the Muslims on the Croats. In effect, he was not interested in what I was saying." Did you hear anything in that audio of President Tudjman referring to crimes committed by Muslims against Croats?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: In the beginning, he had a long -- long history of what has happened in the future, and talking about the crimes during the earlier times. So that it was quite clear that he wanted to -- to raise this question, too; that it is not only the Croat who is were guilty but there are on all sides. So I would say that there were no surprises for me when listening now 13 years later to this -- this audio tape of our discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, where you said what happened in the future, I take it was a slip of the tongue and that you wanted to say what happened in the past.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In the past. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me, Mrs. Rehn, that his opening or his introduction concerning the background of the conflict, that was his statement before you began --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just for technical reasons, we have to speak one at a time, so that the court reporter can record your -- my question and your answer. But you do agree, then, that his reference to Muslims was in the overall context of his discussion about what had happened over the previous four years, and that was in his remarks to you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes. Then, of course, also, you know, the question of the Kuplensko camp, and that was what was actual then, that was referring to -- to two groups of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But you also would now agree that President Tudjman spoke of that camp because you had specifically asked him --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- about --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Absolutely, it was so important, as the case for human rights at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just to the Trial Chamber understands what we're talking about, this was a situation of Bosnian Muslim refugees near the Bihac pocket who had escaped a conflict with other Bosnia Muslims, the Bosnia Muslim army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes. And you will know that it was those who were the so-called Abdic followers who had escaped from the Bihac region, and the -- there were thousands of them in the camp in -- in Kuplensko.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just point out, it is -- the reference to the long history is not before Mrs. Rehn started. According to the transcript I have here, that is transcript page number 2, the -- the second slot. There a long narration by Mr. Tudjman about the history in response to a question by Mrs. Rehn. So it not in the oral context. It is in response specifically to a question raised by Mrs. Rehn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you refer to the second page of the transcript, I think it has the audio and the transcript has not yet been tendered into evidence; so, therefore, the Chamber has no transcript available at this moment because that comes up once we have it. We've only seen it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, A, I don't think that was my point; B I think -- I will tender it, of course, but obviously for counsel, if she has a different spin on what she wants to say, she has more than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that what Ms. Mahindaratne did is that you misrepresented this. That's your point, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is not a matter of how to interpret --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I disagree that I misrepresented it. My point was that the discussion of burning and looting took place after the discussion about the Muslim Croat conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there were two instances. Mrs. Rehn, you have at least a transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm in a good position, in that sense. I really asked before the long story from President Tudjman started, I asked about the looting, the houses that were burned up, we should come over this situation. I mention all these crimes that had been committed, and then President Tudjman's long historical overview took place. I'm grateful for the Prosecution for making me observant because I was just believing that there was a right -- right remark from the Defence. And now when I'm checking this situation, I really was bringing this to President Tudjman and then he started. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, we can debate this back and forth, Your Honour. What Mrs. Rehn says on the transcript is I believe a more general statement, that she doesn't want to be just a bookkeeper, but she wants to face the future and just work together for better understanding in the future of human rights, instead of just telling that those were murder there, those were looted, those were their houses burned up, and they are in mass graves. We should come over this situation. And then President Tudjman starts to start talking about the overall context, so I don't believe it is accurate to say like Ms. Mahindaratne did that this was a discussion about Operation Storm and that something was posed to President Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was about crimes, but not in a very precise context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is again for redirect if she wishes to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... let's leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just suggest, so that the Chamber could follow the discussions and the questions posed to the witness, that if counsel intends to tender this document into evidence to please -- I cannot, of course, ask counsel to do that, but I think it would be appropriate for the Chamber to follow what is going on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we have the text on the transcript, but it would be easier for us to have the transcript in hard copy as well. But let's at this moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I believe I'm going to tender both, and that is my intention. That is why I brought it into court. So, yes, I tender both the audio and the transcript, and the transcript is 1D -- sorry. The clip is 1D40-0087, and that is the transcript as well, I'm advised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is it all under one number. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then, Mr. Registrar, audio and transcript together?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, after the assignment of exhibit numbers in the internal memorandum, the next exhibit number would be D681.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D681 is admitted into evidence. I further inform the parties that during the break, the lack of French translation has been verified. It's lacking only when, for a second time, the same words were spoken.
