So everything that has been said, apart perhaps from some details, because in the translation there might be slight but very minor discrepancies or differences, that we have a French transcript reflecting what was said in the audio. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, turning now to the issue of the general amnesty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, Mr. Registrar, if could I call up 1D33-0325, and if we could go to page 8 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a report of the Secretary-General from 14 February 1996 on the situation on -- of human rights in Croatia. And at paragraph 30, it says: "On 31 December 1995, the president of Croatia issued a decree granting amnesty to 451 Serbs held in prison since last summer on charges of armed rebellion for their alleged military support of the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina. According to the ICRC, 103 persons were released immediately from prison, while 348 others were transferred to the Gasinci refugee camp in eastern Croatia where they were interviewed by ICRC officials. In accordance with their wishes, 306 of this latter group were transported with ICRC assistance to the federal republic of Yugoslavia, while the remainder were released in Croatia. The decision of the Croatian government to grant amnesty to these individuals was noted with appreciation by the Security Council in its presidential statement of 8 January 1996." Mrs. Rehn, were you aware that three weeks after this conversation that you had with President Tudjman in which he spoke of reconciliation, granting amnesty to Serbs, that he, in fact, then acted on what he had said to you by issuing an amnesty to Serbs who had been imprisoned during and after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: I believe that I have reported on this amnesty, and that people were released. So that's totally true, and I'm, of course, not taking in any case the honour to me that it was happening and our conversation. That was, of course, something that was -- was planned, and I have never denied that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am not -- you shouldn't assume that I think you're denying things. I'm just trying to get your best recollection.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm totally aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'll pull up a document, if necessary, but let me just ask you generally: You are aware that in your report of 14 March 1996, you personally, at paragraphs 72 and 109, recommended an amnesty for all former combatants of the former of the Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Mm-hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we're talked about whether common crimes were covered by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I need to call up, Mr. Registrar, 1D33-0316, and if we could go to page 9 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a report of the Secretary-General pursuant to Security Council Resolution 1025, dated 13 December 1995. So it's a little more than a week after your visit with President Tudjman. And at paragraph 25 the last sentence, the Secretary-General writes: "I believe that the implementation of the civilian tasks foreseen in the agreement would be made considerably easier if the parties could agree on an amnesty and exception from prosecution for certain categories of offences excluding war crimes." Are you familiar on the basis of this document of what categories of offences were referred to there by the Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: No. I'm definitely not a lawyer, so that I -- I couldn't just exactly tell that this and this and this crimes are of the kind that are outside the amnesty. So, in that sense, it's difficult for me to answer this question. I -- I would like to say -- make it quite honestly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll go further with some additional reports, and maybe it will refresh your recollection, Mrs. Rehn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D40-0015, please, and if we could go to page 6 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the further report on the situation of human rights in Croatia pursuant to Security Council Resolution 109, dated 5 March 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll to paragraph 22 at the bottom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The Secretary-General writes: "As noted in previous reports, a general amnesty law approved by the parliament of Croatia entered into force on 3 October 1996. The legislation applies to persons accused of or sentenced for criminal acts committed in connection with aggression, rebellion, or armed conflict between 17 August 1990 and 23 August 1996. Criminal investigations or proceedings related to such acts were to be cancelled, and any detained persons who to whom the amnesty applied were to be released. The legislation exempted from its coverage alleged perpetrators of war crimes."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please, and paragraph 24, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "In the region at present administered by UNTAES, the application of the amnesty law continues to cause widespread concern among the Serb population. At the time of writing of the present report, the Croatian authorities were preparing a definitive list of persons believed by them to be in the region and who, in the eyes of the Ministry of Justice, are not covered by the amnesty law. All those not on the list may then consider themselves as amnestied?" And the last sentence, talking about the minister of justice, he stated that: "The final list of war crime suspect would be released as soon as possible." And, finally, in the paragraph 25 there, starting at the second sentence: "The Croatian government has a clear interest in detaining and prosecuting persons reasonably suspected of war crimes. However, appeals have been made to the government, including by the Special Rapporteur of the Commission on Human Rights to finalise its list of war crime suspects on the basis of existing evidence, to remove uncertainty and ensure that arbitrary arrests are not made among Serbs returning to Croatia."

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, reading this document, does that refresh your recollection about the fact that not only were ordinary crimes covered by the amnesty law, but that the international community was asking Croatia actually to prepare a list of people who weren't covered by the amnesty law and who may have been responsible for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question. What we saw was that the amnesty covered acts of aggression, rebellion, or armed conflict. We did not see any reference to ordinary crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is false judge, but if she wants to read what it says, then read what it says. It says: "Acts committed in connection with aggression, armed conflict." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic may put the question to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm in trouble now, because this is very much about judiciary and legal questions that are far beyond my -- my knowledge. To my memory, we were very strong about that it was important that real crimes should not be taken away to be amnestied. Therefore, I'm a little bit surprised for this, that there even could be a question of that -- that crimes committed during this Operation Storm and otherwise too, that they could be amnestied. Perhaps I should give an explanation still on the work of the Special Rapporteur. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am sorry. I have a series of documents, so I think it is probably most fair to you if I show you the documents and then let you comment on ... [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Okay. Do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may the witness complete her answer she wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, what Mr. Misetic suggested, and which is a fair way of dealing with the matter, is that he first finishes his line of questions, and then if there would be any -- if the witness would to explain anything further, that she does that after the questions have been put to her, and that's fair. Mr. Misetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then what I will do is I will call up a series of documents, and then I will put the question to you, Mrs. Rehn, after you have had a chance to see all the documents?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, may I tender this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D682.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D682 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I may call up 1D40-0025, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a statement by the president of the Security Council, 19 March 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to page 2, top paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "The Security Council calls upon the government of Croatia to remove uncertainty about the implementation of its amnesty law; in particular, by finalising without delay the list of war crime suspects on the basis of existing evidence and in strict accordance with international law, and to put an end to arbitrary arrests particularly of Serbs returning to Croatian."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I tendered this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, may I take it that there is no objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D683.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D683 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can now call up 1D40-0027.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, this is your report of 31 October 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to - just a minute - paragraph 58, which is page 15 of this document, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, you write at paragraph 58, speaking of the amnesty law now: "The legislation applies to persons accused of or sentenced for criminal acts committed in connection with aggression, rebellion, or armed conflict between 17 August 1990 and 23 August 1996. Criminal investigation or proceedings related to such acts were to be nullified, and any detained persons to whom the amnesty applied were to be released. The legislation exempted from its coverage alleged perpetrators of war crimes." Paragraph 59, you then recall the presidential statement which I just showed you of 19 March 1997, calling upon the government of Croatia to remove uncertainty about the implementation of its amnesty law, "I particular by finalising without delay its list of war crime suspects on the basis of existing evidence and in strict accordance with international law, and to put an end to arbitrary arrested particularly of Serbs returning to Croatia. The application of the amnesty law, however, continues to cause widespread concern among the Serbian population."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then if we turn to page 23 of this document, at paragraph 98:

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "The government's final list of 150 suspected war criminals, however, has not had the intended effect, i.e., building confidence among the Serb population. People remain uncertain as to the exact content and real meaning of the list. According to the UNTAES statements," and UNTAES being the acronym for UN Transitional Administration of Eastern Slavonia, "all those not on the list should consider themselves immune from future prosecution for war-related crimes." Now, Mrs. Rehn, this is in your report from the 31st of October, 1997. So does this refresh your recollection of the fact that the international community, in order to encourage Serbs to stay in Croatia, wanted the broadest possible amnesty law passed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Due to -- to this report, it is correct, but you left some sentences out, where I -- I strongly took to discussion the fact that this is creating a lot of unrest with the Serb population, because they don't know if they are safe or not because of all the different lists. There is also this UNTAES. I'm -- I'm a referring to UNTAES statements, that means that this is not my report . It is an UNTAES statement that I'm referring to. It's not my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But on direct examination, you weren't asked for your opinion. You were asked what the position of the international community was, which is why I'm putting to you UNTAES being a part of the international community, and I actually agree with what you just said. Meaning, in order -- because there was anxiety among the Serb population as to who is covered or not covered by the amnesty law, would you agree with me that the international community insisted that Croatia prepare a list of people who were suspected of war crimes and that everybody who wasn't on the list could consider themselves amnestied for all crimes committed in connection with the armed conflict, even if later it was discovered that they had committed war crimes?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: I think this was quite a leading question, and still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, that is permitted in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But let me reflect on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are referring here, as I already said before, to UNTAES statements, where they are of the opinion that everybody should be -- a senior Croatian government said that a list doesn't exist, and there are very many different opinions on this. I would say that it was very difficult at that time to get a special opinion of the international community. What is the international community? That is a question we have got so many times put to us, because there are different opinions. We wanted to have an amnesty, but definitely not in a way that could put somebody in danger for perhaps not being guaranteed amnesty; and, on the other hand, to -- to make it quite clear, that nobody can just escape with a war crime and even a very, very strong civil crime, like murdering and burning houses. So I think that it was even a part of my discussion with President Tudjman, if I may recall rightly, that these are very tricky questions; and to just ask for one international community opinion at that time with all the problems, I think that would be impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, may I ask you: Will you present at any later stage the list in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We are in the process of obtaining it from the Ministry of Justice, but there were several lists that were circulated, and we're in the process of getting the final list that was turned over to the UN Transitional Authority in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it should shed some light on what I see at this moment as a bit of a problem. From what I understand, but please correct me if I'm wrong, Mrs. Rehn, from what I understand you express concern about the bad things that you had seen happening and that no prosecutions took place. I understood this to be, but again, correct me if I'm wrong, bad things committed by Croats during or after Operation Storm. That's when you were talking about the looting and the burning. Now, the whole line of questioning now shifts to what seems to be not exactly the same problem, which is that Serbs were fearing that, upon return, they might be prosecuted, and that they had some concerns about whether they would be prosecuted for actively taking part in whether you call it rebellion, at least being members of enemy forces, more or less, to Croatia. Now, what would assist me is to find out whether this, I would say perhaps, implicit coverage, because not excluded Croats having committed war crimes, if they were committed, whether that was the issue you wanted to raise; or whether the focus, was, when you raised the issue with President Tudjman, on the clear distinction between Serbs having participated in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't think -- sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would assist me to have a clearer view on that, and that's also the reason why I'm asking about these lists, because if that would be a clearly mixed list, then it could shed some light on the issue which is puzzling me at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may respond to that, Your Honour. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that is my concern, and then, of course, you can put questions to the witness, and at least you know what would assist me in better understanding this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm actually not sure what the issue is. You're looking for the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the list could be one element of having a clearer view on what puzzles me, but also what Mrs. Rehn raised with President Tudjman and what exactly the new legislation and the list were focussing on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe I can comment because it is now all in evidence, Your Honour, that the legislation as drafted and as the actual amnesty law I have tendered into evidence, which is 1D33-0495 - I believe it has a number now - was, as you know, in a democratic society, the laws apply equally. It is also incorrect to say that the international community was interested in an amnesty for rebellion crimes, which is precisely why I took her through these documents. The whole point was that the international community insisted that any crime, burning, looting, theft, et cetera, except - and you can read the law as to what was excluded - that was connected to the armed conflict was amnestied. The law applies, as in any democratic country, not on the basis of who's an ethnic member of one group or not, it applies -- equal protection of the law applies. And it was, as I might add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, Mr. Misetic. I'm not in a debate with you at this moment. What I said is that there was an element in the line of questioning and the testimony of the witness which I was struggling with; and for you to know that I was struggling with it, might guide you in seeking further to clarify these issues. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, you have heard some of the discussion of the policy behind encouraging the amnesty law. And let me, again, restate - and we had this in response to your last answer - about what is the international community. You would agree with me that the Security Council, in terms of the international community, is one of the highest instances, if not the highest instance, of the representative body that speaks for the international community. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So, again, 19 March 1997: "The president of the Security Council calls upon the government of Croatia to remove uncertainty about the implementation of its amnesty law, in particular by finalising without delay the list of war crime suspects on the basis of existing evidence and in strict accordance with international law." I'm going to try to address the question that was posed by Judge Orie. But the policy behind the Security Council calling upon Croatia to do this was to eliminate any uncertainty for Serbs about their future in Croatia, so that people would not fear that if they returned, they would be arrested for a crime. Whether it was armed rebellion, theft, some other common crime, the international community through the Security Council wanted Serbs to have certainty as to what laws would apply to them. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in conjunction with that policy, Croatia, you're aware, passed an amnesty act. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Mm-hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And are you aware that that amnesty act applied to all citizens of the Republic of Croatia and not just citizens who may be ethnic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Of course, because there are other minorities, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And there are majorities, too?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Sorry. There are other minorities, too, and majorities. There are other nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if I tendered the 31 October 1997 report of Mrs. Rehn, but if I haven't, I tender it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me give Mr. Registrar the number, 1D40-0027.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D684.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D684 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, while I'm on this topic, I am going to pull up a document just to tender from the bar table on this amnesty issues, which may be relevant to the Trial Chamber for reasons that I won't go in to, but it is 1D40-0093.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an ECMM report received by the Gotovina Defence from 9 August 1995. And in the third paragraph, we have: "A," deletion, "met with," deletion, "who stated that the number of the Croatian fatalities during Operation Storm was 118, and that the Serb losses were not very high because the HV had not met strong Serb resistance. He added that detained Krajina soldiers who have not committed war crimes will be amnestied within one month."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, unfortunately, the redactions were not made by us. This is one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. So, Your Honour, I'd ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D685.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D685 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Rehn, I'm going to turn your attention now to your meeting with Minister Susak on the 4th of December. And in your statement, you make reference to the fact that -- let me call it up. At page 5, you say: "Susak defended the Croatian military by making reference to my report and saying that I should have concentrated more on the civilians who commited crimes in my earlier report, instead of pointing out that crimes were committed by the Croatian military. I pointed out that my report was based on the facts that been collected by internationals in the field, and some of those situations had been personally observed by me. He was dissatisfied with my report and my response." Now, I'd like to pull up your 7 November report, which I still have as 65 ter 2710. And I note in your statement, Mrs. Rehn, at page 2, you said: "I prepared reports for the Security Council based on information from many organisations, including ECMM, ICRC, and other human rights organisations. This would include UNPROFOR, UNMO, and UNCIVPOL representatives. My staff would both interview people and check the information before I would report it." Is that how this report of the 7th of November was prepared by gathering information from other international organisations?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes. All my reports are -- were prepared in that way, with personal discussions, with the talking with people on the grass root level with -- with the political leadership; and then gathering information from all the human rights organisations and -- and the UN and other organisations in the field; also, very strongly the national Croatian human rights organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mrs. Rehn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 5 of the report, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 9, the Secretary-General reports: "During her first mission to Croatian, the Special Rapporteur was informed by international observers and representatives of local non-governmental organisations about the status of the various human rights problems persisting in that country. Her mission was also devoted to establishing important contacts with relevant authorities. In future missions, the Special Rapporteur intends to conduct her own first-hand investigations of alleged human rights violations." Now, the way this is phrased, is it fair to say that this report is not on the basis of any first-hand investigation that you had done, and that, instead, you were going to do a first-hand investigation with a subsequent report?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: No, that is totally wrong. It is a wrong interpretation of this, because I made studies. I went to Sector North. I met with people who had been left there. I could myself observe terrible things. So that was totally incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to page seven of the report, please. At paragraph 15, you say: "During the military operation, civilian targets including residential areas of Knin were deliberately targeted by the Croatian army."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We can stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What evidence did you have when you prepared this report that the Croatian army deliberately targeted civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: There is, for instance, the Grubori case that I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. This is now talking about during the military action --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- so during the ... [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, sorry. These are reports that I have got from my staff of the human rights commission, and what they have got through their cooperation with other UN organisations. So, in that sense, it is firsthand -- first-hand information delivered to the Special Rapporteur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: And, sooner or later, I would like to have the possibility to, with a few words, inform the Court about the way and the independence of a human rights rapporteur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, you will have an opportunity to do so. Would this be a suitable moment, Mr. Misetic. I don't want to interrupt your --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me finish this line of questioning, Mrs. Rehn, and then we'll give you an opportunity to speak to that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could, while we have the document on the screen, turn to page 8, which is the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 23, it says: "Evidence gathered so far indicates that violations of human rights and humanitarian law which were committed during and after Operation Storm include the following:" And then B says: "Targeting of heavy weapons against militarily insignificant sites in towns, including residence areas of Glina and Knin." Now, was this also information that had been obtained by your staff?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could I have P64 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, this is an UNMO report from the 18th of August, so it is several months before your report. Paragraph 1 -- actually, the title or underneath the date is: "Provisional assessment of damage caused by HV operations from the 4th to the 6th of August, 1995 at Knin. UNMO team Podkonje has made a provisional assessment of the damages caused by the HV operations from 04 to 06 August 1995, in the town of Knin. The report is based on a run down of 70 per cent of Knin town, and gives only a brief overview of the situation." Paragraph 2 says: "In general, shelling was concentrated against military objectives. The damages caused by shelling to civilian establishments is concentrated to the close vicinity of military objectives. Only three to five impacts is observed in other urban areas."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn -- call up P228, Mr. Registrar. This is an UNCIVPOL assessment of damage in Knin town caused by the Croat liberation, dated 18 August 1995. It says : "Friday, 18 August 1995, at 10.30, together with investigation officer, Thor Hansen, I started a survey of Knin town to assess the damage down in Knin town caused by shelling, arson, and wilful damage. "We covered the whole township and observed several impacts of shells/rockets around the Tvik factory, Milicija headquarters," milicija meaning police, "general direction of north barracks, shells coming from the north-east, and between the government house, Knin radio/TV building, and the hillside below Knin castle. The compound of north barracks was not checked. Observation done from street level. "We counted roughly 20 houses, buildings hit by shells and about another 20 presumable damaged by arson," and then it goes on. Mrs. Rehn, when you were preparing your report, was the UNCIVPOL report of the 18th of August, 1995, and the UNMO report of the 18th of August, 1995, was that available for your review before reaching the conclusions that you placed in your report?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: It is impossible for me to recall. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was waiting for the French translation to be finished, otherwise that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that, yes, this is totally impossible for me to recall which were the special documents on -- on every occasion and for every paragraph of my reports. You must remember that I was not only covering Croatia. That was only a small part of my mission. So that now just answer did this documents be there as a basis for my report on this specific paragraph, it is impossible for me to recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you had access to those reports from UNMO and UNCIVPOL, do you think that would have affected your conclusion in your report that the Croatian army deliberately targeted civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object to that question, Mr. President, because there have been other evidence led in this court, and to ask about these two documents in isolation is unfair. Already, the witness has indicated that she cannot recall what reports she reviewed which was the basis for her conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is argument and not a legitimate objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the Chamber is not assisted by putting a question to a witness where she has made a report on the basis of, at this moment, unspecified information, unspecified to the extent that the general source is known, but not the details of that; then to put one or two examples of reports to the witness and then ask her with she would have changed her mind not having been in a position to review all the information. To that extent, the objection by Ms. Mahindaratne is justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it makes it really difficult to cross-examine when they tender a report and then say the witness doesn't know the basis of the conclusions in her own report, and any questions put to her on existing evidence that we have is outside the scope. I don't understand of submitting the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said it doesn't assist the Chamber. I hope you understand what that primary means, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Rehn, if you would like to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps now is a the moment when I should clarify a little more about the work of a Special Rapporteur on human rights. We have many of them around in the world. They are totally independent. They are not dependant on the United Nations. They are not, in that sense, a part of the United Nations. They are not even having a salary from the United Nations for their work. It is a so-called honorary mission. There is a staff from the human rights commission - that it used to be earlier; it has a new name now - and who are assisting the Special Rapporteur, who are making field trips, who are interviewing other organisations, who are cooperation, and who are lawyers have all these details clear. What is important is that the human rights report to the United Nations is based on common sense and what are the impressions of the Special Rapporteur. It is apparently regarded that that person is a person of some integrity and reliable. And, therefore, the methods have been like this. Security Council commission are giving their answers on resolutions on the reports and then picking up some important questions. I have already made quite clear that judiciary is not my strong part; human rights are, definitely, and the position of individuals in difficult situations. But I don't doubt and I don't want to doubt my sources my people. You were talking about the shelling with artillery on civilian sites. But in the report by the UNMOs, there were mentioned in general, no outside military compounds, but with three to five different situations, that were possible. So it was not totally absolute with that statement. I would say that these reports are very important, giving an overview of the suffering of ordinary people and the answers and -- and the steps they are getting from the political leadership. So in that sense, we must have it clear for us what is the real role of a report. And when saying this, I'm definitely not telling that they should not be reliable. On the contrary. They are very reliable. But they are giving one voice to the misery; in this case, after a very, very, brutal war. Still, with the list where you tried to make me a little bit unconvincing with the lists and the -- and the amnesty, it would be quite easy for us to understand that what I was especially talking about and asking about in Croatia at that time was the situation of the Serb population and what had happened to them. I had all the possibilities in the other parts of the former Yugoslavia to look at crimes committed against Croats, Muslims, and so on. So even I would say that, of course, I did not mean personally an amnesty that would exclude those who have committed severe crimes. Why should I otherwise have raised the question and the case of Grubori so many times and asked for answers? So I hope this is -- I'm very sorry for taking so much of the time up of the Court, but it was important for me to give an explanation the way the Rapporteur is working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no need to apologise, Mrs. Rehn, for giving the explanation. Could I put one question to you. Mr. Misetic has put to you the line where it say: "Evidence gathered so far indicates that violations of human rights and humanitarian law committed during and after Operation Storm, include the following ..." and then: "B, targeting of heavy weapons against militarily insignificant sites in towns, including residence areas of Glina and Knin." He also has put to you the -- well, he has put this to you. Were your sources unanimous on these matters, because, as you may have noticed, Mr. Misetic, has presented to you some reports with -- which -- tend to go in the direction that targeting was mainly against military targets and that impacts were at least close to military targets. My question is: Were your sources unanimous at that time, or did you include, when reporting, also reports which would not fully be in line with your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course what I concluded in my reports were reports given to me on what those persons had experienced themselves. And as I already mentioned, at least in the report by UNMOs to -- to Mr. Misetic, there was three to five exceptions to this with the military targets that there could have been three to five military -- non-military targets that were shot at. You will find it somewhere in your -- in your papers that you just presented to us. And, so, it's difficult for me to give a totally covering answer to you, Your Honour, because when we discussed what will be included in the report - and when I'm saying "we," it was the team of the Human Rights Commission's field operation - so we are many discussing this. And of course it was a question of our honour to -- not to just give false information because it would have been against our interests. So I have to stand for those opinions expressed and the firsthand information expressed by my interlocutors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's no question about thinking at this moment that you would give a false impression. I'm just trying to find out exactly how you work. For example -- let me put it in an example. If you would receive 98 reports saying that, for example, shelling was indiscriminate or against civilian targets, and there would be two reports saying, no, targeting was mainly focussing on military targets, would you have then concluded that by such a vast majority that shelling was indiscriminate and would you have mention that as a conclusion, or would you have made a footnote saying that -- I am trying to find out to what extent reports which are not -- are not fully supportive of your conclusions are -- were considered and whether they were explicitly mentioned if they were there, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really hope that I have been able to do as Your Honour advised that I should have been doing, that there could have been footnotes on some unclear cases, but I can't recall that we should have -- had even a discussion that there are other opinions on -- on the things we reported on, because we got our lists, we knew who has been there, who had seen it, and it was a long, long, long list of different cases that we put together. We put our -- our questions to authorities on different levels to get confirmation, and then, of course, so much of course we were tricky, or I personally, that depending on that if the perpetrator was telling that this is not true, who we thought that could be, the perpetrator, then we didn't put so much perhaps strength on -- on that other opinion. But I would say that our reporting was very fair, and if something was very unclear -- and sometimes, of course, I had to -- to make my own decisions that they should not mention this, is it really clear enough, and then we should not mention it because it's better to have an accurate report than to have any fancy things. What was that line was all together with the reports was quite tough wherever I reported from, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, Kosovo, Serbia, Croatia, former Republic of Macedonia, it was a tough language, because I had to -- to wake up people. That is the function of the rapporteur, to wake up people, that something is not as it should be. It was not the diplomatic language, and I could use that language when I spoke with people, but not in reports. So with quite a long answer, I would say that, to the best of my knowledge, these were accurate reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could get 65 ter 2710 back on the screen at page 27, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, this is page 27 of your 7 November 1995 report. And at paragraph 105, you write: "Serious human rights violations and violations of humanitarian law were perpetrated by members of the Croatian army during and after Operation Storm in the former Sectors North and South." Now, at the end of this report there's an appendix which identifies persons you met with on your travels from the 9th of October, 1995 through the 14th of October, 1995 in the region, and it notes that on Thursday, October 12th, you had a meeting with Mr. Peter Galbraith, Ambassador of the United States of America. And I'd like to call your attention to the fact that Mr. Galbraith testified before this Trial Chamber on the 24th of June, 2008, at page 4985. He was asked: "So it was your conclusion" --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could, I think we have an agreement here that even if witnesses are presented with testimonies of other witnesses that this witness in court is asked to present his or her position on a particular issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Ms. Mahindaratne, the question arose yesterday when Mr. Hedaraly raised the issue. The ruling at that time was if a matter had not been dealt with in examination-in-chief or in the evidence already given, so to that extent it is more or less the introduction of a new document and not just cross-examination in response of the -- then we should elicit from the witness first independent on any other documents. But I think, as a matter of fact, that Mr. Misetic is here cross-examining on matters on which the witness, although through 92 ter, testified in examination-in-chief, and then there's no need to reintroduce that element, but in cross-examination I would say in the -- in the limited sense, it is no problem to put to the question -- to the witness what other evidence contains which was presented to the chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galbraith testified before this Trial Chamber, and he was asked: "So it was your conclusion that the actual attack in Operation Storm in the -- in these first few days was consistent with international humanitarian law. Is that right? "Answer: I don't think there were major violations of international humanitarian law in those first few days." Mrs. Rehn, at paragraph 105 here, you say that during the operation there were violations of humanitarian law. Do you recall if Ambassador Galbraith, in your meeting with him on the 12 October 1995, advised you of his view that there were no major violations of international humanitarian law during the operation itself.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: I remember that we had talks about a lot of -- of problems in -- around the Operation Storm. It is impossible for me to remember what exactly we talked about. If I remember rightly, he offered me a nice dinner, but that is something else. But he, of course, is standing for his own opinion, and I'm representing my opinion. So, certainly, if he thinks that there are no major violations of international humanitarian law, I think that all violations against human individuals are a violation. But I can't recall that we specifically talked about this. We talked around all what happened then, and I think we were very much of the same opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Going back, then, to your meeting with Minister Susak on the 4th, it is true, is it not, that Minister Susak was dissatisfied with the conclusions in your report, that the Croatian army deliberately targeted civilians during the operation. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: It is stated here in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I checked 4985, which is the first page of the 24th of June, I do not find it there. It should be another page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 5043, Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It was also Minister Susak's opinion during your meeting with him that during Operation Storm there were no major violations of international humanitarian law. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes, that was his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there was some discussion about evictions from apartments. You were asked about that by Ms. Mahindaratne. The issue there, you will recall, was not evictions of ordinary Serbs from their homes, correct, the issue was evictions of former Yugoslavia national army officers from apartments that now belonged to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: I would say so, but I think there were also ordinary Serbs. But this is something I'm -- I'm not totally clear with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Those --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: These are details 13 years behind that I just can't recognise and remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Those ordinary people in the apartments, would they have been family of the military person?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: I think we have a long list of these evictions. I don't have it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It was brought up this morning that during the course of these evictions sometimes violence would take place. Do you recall whether this violence took place in -- in the process of executing a court order to evict people from military apartments?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: I can't remember that I would have that there was violence with this. My problem was more with all these evictions from the military apartments, that there was a contradiction between what Minister of the Interior Jarnjak told me, and what Susak told me who was present and so on. The violence I always been referring to has been in -- in connection with the return of Serbs to their homes in the few cases when they have been able to return than in the begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that would have been a subject that you addressed with the minister of the interior, Mr. Jarnjak, correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: These were evictions from military. That is something that is in my report. I think we have it here in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: -- in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. What I'm saying is you would have these conversations about evictions from military apartments with Minister Susak?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes, and with Jarnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the general issue of violence against Serbs, you had those conversations primarily with the minister of the interior, Mr. Jarnjak?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: I had it also with Minister Susak. You must remember that we were old colleagues. I had met him earlier in 1993, and I met him without all these procedures on some occasions in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your notes of your meeting with Minister Susak, it's mentioned that Minister Susak told you that 220 criminal proceedings were undertaken concerning arson and looting.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that what Minister Susak said?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: If it is stated here, then, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did that indicate to you that Minister Susak acknowledged that criminal prosecutions were necessary for illegal conduct conducted -- or committed after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Mm-hm, certainly. But not very interested in the matter as a whole with the civilian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could that be because Minister Susak felt it was not part of his portfolio to be prosecuting and --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: I hope so, that he had a clear understanding of -- of portfolio of his ministry and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this might be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you done with 65 ter 2710?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that you wanted to tender that into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne tendered it this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It is part of the 92 ter submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen that. Yes, it would be P639, although still marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I need to print out the list during the break, Your Honours, because I don't have the numbers with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you used it and since Ms. Mahindaratne tendered it, I think the status of P639 could already be changed in the absence of any objections of any of the other parties in an exhibit. We'll have a break and resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, now I'd like to talk to you about your meeting with Minister Jarnjak on 4 December 1995. This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit P601 on the screen, please. That's the one, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Rehn, in your statement, you discuss your meeting with Minister Jarnjak, and you say -- let me find the page for you. At page 6, you say: "Jarnjak claimed that he did not have data on humanitarian abuses, and it was clear to me that he did not want to receive the information from us. Jarnjak also indicated that he was not going to investigate the reports of mass graves." Now, if we look at the notes, at paragraph 2, it's noted that: "Minister Jarnjak replied that the security situation ..." -- I should say section 2. "Minister Jarnjak replied that the security situation has normalised and criminal proceedings have been undertaken against perpetrators of crimes commited, i.e., looting, arson," et cetera. And then if we go to page 3, specifically about this issue about him not having data on humanitarian abuses -- sorry, on page 2. I apologise. I couldn't find it. Page 2, paragraph -- or section 7, it says: "Regarding the situation on the return of refugees, she raised her concern about many administrative obstacles which did not facilitate the return of refugees. She inquired whether data available on a number of returns. "Minister Jarnjak mentioned did he not have any data on that matter and did not receive any comments concerning human rights abuses after the return of refugees. He recognised that the difficulties occurring after their return are connected to problems existing between neighbours." So, is it fair to say that what Minister Jarnjak said at the meeting was not that he had no data on humanitarian abuses; but, rather, that he no data on humanitarian abuses against refugee who had returned to the area?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Of course, you can put your words in that way. I think that we, both of us, understand what was meant in the report and in my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking, Mrs. Rehn, because --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm just telling that he didn't have data on what I was asking about, the returns and the humanitarian abuses around this; and so, in that sense, it is an answer on the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you say, he didn't have --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: It is written here. He didn't have the data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He didn't have the data on abuses occurring against people who had returned. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was not the answer. The witness clearly answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne. Mrs. Rehn, you have understood, I take it, what Mr. Misetic is concerned about. What matters exactly is did Mr. Jarnjak tell you he had no data. If you could explain that, and refer to part of the notes you consider relevant, then, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked about the returnees; and as we talked about them, he said that he don't have data. So it could be, of course, taken as an overall that he is in possession of any kind of data, but it was definitely with reference to the return of the refugees and human rights abuses around these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meaning about around the return and not prior to the return? I mean unrelated to the return, perhaps I should say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour, to say that I can't answer this question because it's some time ago, and the notes taken by Mr. Diakite are not very clear in this sense. But what I have as my memory from those discussions was that he was not very much interested in the problems created by the returns and also in the civilian casualties in connection to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With regard to the last portion of your answer, Mrs. Rehn, do you have anything in the notes that would reflect that Mr. Jarnjak was not interested in the civilian casualties in connection to Operation Storm? Is there any reference you can give us in the notes?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: No, only my head, and that is something that you can't just make a reference to, unfortunately. But so much of the reports are based on -- on discussions, on talks with people, because you know very well that in the minutes of the meeting, you are not putting every, every word in the minutes. So that was the impression I had when I came out from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Turning to the next page of these notes, please, it's section 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This relates to the statement in your statement that: "Jarnjak indicated that he was not going to investigate reports of mass graves." Paragraph 11 says: "The Special Rapporteur expressed her concern on the situation of mass graves which should be investigated now or soon after in the former Yugoslavia. She pointed out that police from both sides should attend those events for investigation and monitoring, i.e., international observers for more impartiality and as to avoid any confusion in the result. "Minister Jarnjak explained that the parliament adopted a legislation by which all information on war crimes should be forwarded to the international war crimes Tribunal. He said that they will ensure all necessary measures for more transparency in that matter."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then it continues on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "The Special Rapporteur mentioned also that it is important to preserve the dignity of those persons when opening the graves and to facilitate the presence of religious authorities; i.e., bishop, orthodox priest. Minister Jarnjak fully supported the suggestion, and add that so far only allegations on mass graves have been reported against Croatia, referring to the allegation in Pakrac. And the international community was invited, and they await results from that investigation on that matter. However, he pointed out that in the liberated areas, they have indications of mass graves in some areas." Could you point or tell us the basis for your statement that Minister Jarnjak indicated that he would not investigate mass graves?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: It was the overall impression I got from what he said. That is also written in this paragraphs, that, okay, "There are perhaps mass graves. There is the law that has been adopted by the -- by the parliament of Croatia," with reference to the international criminal court and the Tribunal. But direct actions, "Everybody is welcome to come" and so on, but not exactly what he is going to do, and that is lacking from these -- these minutes from this meeting. And that was the impression I then got, and I was not alone on that. My -- my fellows accompanying me at that meeting had exactly the same impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: According to the notes, it was you who had framed the issue as one of whether the international observers would be allowed to participate in the investigations of mass graves. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes. Due to these notes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And so all Minister Jarnjak was doing was responding to you that, yes, international observers would be allowed --

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- to participate. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that the results of that investigation according to new Croatian legislation should be forwarded to the war crimes Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes, exactly what is said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now at page 3 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you quoted that the investigation should be forwarded; whereas, the text says "information," which is not exactly the same, because it's exactly the issue raised by Mrs. Rehn, which was what to do yourself, and perhaps to what extent to respond to what others initiated. Otherwise, I would not have pointed that if it was just a minor meaningless distinction between the two words. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On page 3 of your statement, you say -- referring now to your 7 November 1995 report, you say: "On page 14, I refer to the Croatian minister of the interior providing the results of investigations into crimes in connection with Operation Storm. In the figures that were quoted, only one Croatian soldier was mentioned as having been investigated. Because of this, I did not believe the figures because we had ample information to the contrary."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go back to 65 ter 2710, Mr. Registrar, and page 14 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Rehn, this is the page that you refer to in your witness statement, and it -- at paragraph 35, it says, in the second sentence: "On 18 October 1995, the Croatian minister of the interior presented the results of the investigation of crimes committed in connection with Operation Storm, according to the police -- according to which, the police had resolved 25 or 41 registered cases of murder. The police have arrested 13 people suspected of committing crimes in the village of Gosici and in Varivode. According to the government, only one Croatian army soldier was included among the suspects; whereas, all others were civilians who wearing military apparel." Now you interpreted that sentence to mean that the Croatian minister of the interior said that only one Croatian army soldier was mentioned as having been investigated in connection with crimes committed after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, is it possible that the report actually refers to one Croatian army soldier who was among the suspects for the crimes committed in the village of Gosici and in Varivode, and not that there was one Croatian army soldier suspected of crimes -- concerning all crimes after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: It is impossible for me to answer that. Of course, everything could be possible. But this was something that human rights team had paid a lot of attention to, so it's difficult for me to -- to believe that they were not clear in this -- in this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, this is not a sentence of the Croatian government. This is a sentence written by the Secretary-General pursuant to your report.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But it is based on my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, earlier, we talked about the fact that Minister Susak told that you 222 persons had been charged with burning and looting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Mm-hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Minister Susak would have been referring to soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: I would believe so. They have been charged, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you note any -- anything about the fact that, as of 7 November 1995, you apparently are of the opinion that you were reporting that the Croatian authorities had only suspected one soldier for all the crimes committed after Storm, and by 4 December 1995, the minister of defence was telling you that the number was 222?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: That was a number that we could not or I could not check. So it was something that was told to me; and, of course, we had to take it as something that was relevant. But these -- these differences between these numbers, I don't think they are very important. The important is the overall attitude that charges for militaries were not as popular as for the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's talk about that overall attitude. And just like we did this morning, what I'm going to do, in the interests of time, is to show you a series of additional reports by you and by the Secretary-General, and then ask you some questions about that attitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Misetic, could I ask one clarification. One of the questions Mr. Misetic put to you is that whether Minister Susak would have been referring to soldiers, in relation to the 222; and your answer is: "I would believe so. They have been charged, yes." What's the basis for your belief that he was referring to soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he was not talking about any other groups mostly than just the soldiers. He was very strong about this. He was in charge of the defence people obeying the defence and the rules there, and then the others were a mandate for other ministers like the interior and so on. But this is only something I believed, that it could refer to the military. I don't have a relevant answer on that. It's my impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you because in your statement, you express that you were criticised for focussing on soldiers rather than on potential civilian perpetrators of these acts. Of course, I'm asking to what extent you can reconcile this criticism, but at the same time speaking about the relatively large number which you consider to be about soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are really putting now in a thinking mode of what exactly was meant with this, because it is not anything that is not confirmed by my staff that Minister Susak really was not very pleased about the report, about anything that I had done. So, in that sense, we -- we had all the time a feeling that he is not interested in being very helpful to us regarding the military. So now when are you taking this, that should be perhaps the most logic that he referred perhaps to something else that than to military when we took it as military. That's quite open, and I really must say that this is something that is absolutely impossible for me to memorize.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Misetic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- perhaps there are objective data which gives us an opportunity not to rely on logic in conversation, but rather on objective data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There are a lot more witnesses to cross-examine, Your Honour, so it's coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As I said, Mrs. Rehn, we will show you -- I will show you a series of documents now, and ask for -- a few questions at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But if we could call up 65 ter 2365, it should be Mrs. Rehn's report of 14 March 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, 2365 is already marked for identification as D669, but without the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I'm wondering whether it finally will be D669 with a translation, or whether you vacated that number and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that 2365 will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D669. So, then, Ms. Mahindaratne, there is no need anymore to tender 2365. But is there a translation meanwhile, or do you borrow that from --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's an official UN document. I was not aware that we had to translate those.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a translation uploaded of 2365, and I believe it has been given a MFI number P638 MFI. So I leave it with you, Mr. President, as to which document you would prefer to use. Our document has a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's the same to me, Your Honour, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I then suggest since the Defence was first, it will be D669 and that you borrow the translation from 2365, and that, Mr. Registrar, that this P638 can be vacated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to page 26 of the report, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 104, you write: "Information provided by the government of Croatia indicates that a large number of judicial proceedings have been instituted with respect to crimes and human rights violations that were allegedly committed mostly against Croatian Serbs in the aftermath of the military operations. However, many reported cases of killings remain unresolved, and there is little evidence of trials concerning acts of arson or looting being brought to a conclusion."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could call up -- I have the still. I apologise if there are P numbers, but I have 65 ter 2820, which is a report on the situation of human rights in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, dated 12 November 1996, which is, I'm told, P640, MFI [Realtime transcript read in error "P460, MFI"].

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, there's an error on the transcript. It is recorded as "P460," I believe it is "P640."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph -- let me see. This is, again, a report by the Secretary-General, and it is passing along your periodic report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if I look at the transcript again, that "460" is corrected into "460," instead of "640." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At page 33, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 127, the paragraph is in the context of the issue of the property rights and the Croatian property law as an area of concern. The last sentence says: "On the other hand, the government of Croatia should be given credit for positive steps it has taken in cooperation with international agencies to alleviate the humanitarian plight of Croatian Serbs still residing in the form still Sectors West, North, and South, many of whom are elderly." If we go to page 37, paragraph 148, the second sentence begins: "The Republic of Croatia has continuously engaged in constructive cooperation with international entities including the Special Rapporteur and the office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. Croatia's recent acceptance of the presence of an OSCE mission, which will pay special attention to the question of minority rights, is another demonstrations of this cooperation." And then let me call up your January 1998 report, Mrs. Rehn, which is P651 MFI'd. You will note this is the 14 January 1998 report that you submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 9 of the report, please. At paragraph 28, you say, in the middle: "The Special Rapporteur wishes, once again, to thank the Croatian authorities for their constructive cooperation throughout the duration of her mandate." Then at paragraph 29, which a section entitled, "Security of person and property in the former sectors": "After more than two years of observing human rights trends in Croatia, the Special Rapporteur is of the opinion that while more still needs to be accomplished, there are good reasons for optimism for the future. When she first took up her mandate in 1995, serious violations of human rights and humanitarian law were reported to have occurred during and after Croatian military operations in the summer of that year, when the government seized back control over formerly Serb-held territory. These violations, many of which evidently were carried out by Croatian soldiers, had involved killings of civilians, massive looting and burning, and attacks on fleeing civilians and refugees. "According to information recently received from the government, as of October 1997, a total of 5.580 criminal proceedings had been carried out in relation to the military operations carried out in the former Sectors North and South, of which 559 are at the investigative stage, 3.785 are in the first instance proceedings, and 1.236 have been brought through to final decisions."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 34 is talking about the situation in eastern Slavonia. In the middle of the paragraph, you write: "Prior to the conclusion of the UNTAES mandate, on 15 January 1998, Croatian authorities were trying to encourage Croatian Serbs to remain in the region. However, the widespread fear and uncertainty among members of the Serb population reportedly led to a number of departures from the region, mainly for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, although it difficult to ascertain whether such departures are intended to be permanent." Mrs. Rehn, I have shown you some of the statements over the course of 1995, 1996, and to January 1998. Is it fair to say that you saw improvement that led to you say in your January 1998 report that there were -- well, more still needed to be accomplished. There were good reasons for optimism for the future.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, because I had never hesitated to give or to pay credit to those steps that had been taken. I think it is much more important then to also point out that those questions that still are open when you also acknowledge the improvements and through my reports. And if I would make report today about Croatia, definitely it would be even much nicer. So there was a clear development in direction to democracy. It was on my recommendation they institute the Ombudsman institution. I was very pleased about so many steps were taken. But, of course, we are talking now about what happened during the Operation Storm and immediately after. And, therefore, I have been forced to tell also very, very brutal things about the situation. But improvement has been there, as clearly stated in my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And just with respect to the statistics that you cited, I know you have said in your statements that you never were able to verify the statistics. But you don't have any recollection of ever having asked for the underlying court files, to look at the court files in order to investigate the numbers for yourself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: This is very important question, because I have asked it to -- from my myself, that did we, the team, ask for documents from court procedures, and I cannot answer that question because I'm almost sure that my team asked for it. But just, here, in the witness stand, I cannot surely say it. So it is not only because of the lack of interest from the officials of Croatia that we perhaps didn't get it. Perhaps we even didn't ask for these documents forceful enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you think, based on your experience as the Special Rapporteur and the fact that you wrote many reports, do you think that if you, in fact, had asked the Croatian government for such documents and they didn't provide it to you, would that have been something that would have been included in one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Certainly, it would have been. It would have been included. So, in had a sense, it is more likely that we didn't forcefully enough ask for the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mrs. Rehn. I'd like to turn to the area of citizenship rights, page 7 and 8 - and I will try to finish this before we leave today -- 7 and 8 of your statement. You say, beginning on the bottom: "I have no doubt that the practical administrative obstacles faced by the Serb refugees in attempting to return were purposely crafted by the Croatian authorities difficult and to discourage the Serbs from returning. I have no doubt that the Croatian administration of the time did not readily welcome the idea of the return of the Serb refugees who had fled as a consequence of Operation Storm. Under the subheading, 'Humanitarian and social issues,' I address the issue of denial of citizenship rights to long-term residents of Croatia. They were predominantly Serbs." First, do you recall which Serbs who were residents of Croatia were denied citizenship?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me find --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Would you put your question to me again, because I didn't get the point, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
