utterances.text: Let me show you actually where this comes from. It's from that last report that we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go back to that, Mr. Registrar, P651. Now, if we could go to the next page, please, and then if we could go to page 11, please, and if we could scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That portion of your statement comes from this portion of your report of 1998 at paragraph 39 at the bottom. You are talking about Eastern Slavonia, and the second to last sentence on that page says: "Some 140.000 citizenship papers and 126.000 passports have been issued to residents in the region," the region being Eastern Slavonia. "However, concern remains over some 900 denials of citizenship pending for many months ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: " ... in administrative tribunals which need to be effectively resolved?" On the issue of the citizenship, Croatia, as you say in your own report, had, in fact, issued 140.000 citizenship papers to residents in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: In even Slavonia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And there was a problem with approximately 900 denials. Correct? Are you aware of what the basis of the problem was in getting those 900 people citizenship?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: What I have been especially talking about in my statements and in my recalling, because I was not involved approximate Easter Slavonia, in that sense, we had UNTAES administration and I thought that it would be quite appropriate for me that just involve myself too much in what was the administration there. Of course, I visited the area. But my problem was the citizenships and to show, and we have proved of the documents of those who left Sectors North and South during Operation Storm, because many of them lost their papers, ID cards. There were a lot of difficulties for them to just prove that they are citizens of Croatia. And those were the persons that I was especially worried about. I know there was hundreds of them waiting on the Hungarian side to get the papers. They had to go to Belgrade to get some of the papers. And it was practically very difficult for them when trying to get back their property, because they had a 90 days limit within which they should claim for property. So all these were, so to say, attached to each other, and that is what I mostly referred to in my written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We have three minutes.

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry. Let's make it quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am sorry for interrupting you, but I do want to finish this topic today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could, Mr. Registrar, call up 1D40-0082.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you can tell me whether you know, yes or no, but are you aware that in Croatia in this time-period, meaning 1996, 1997, 1998, and previously, a persons citizenship was established by amongst other things his birth records in his local registry office in his local town. Are I aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: Yes. And I know, too, that those who had overtaken Krajina for that are period when they were born, children were born in the Krajina, they often didn't have papers at all because it was not a registered city -- region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is under the citizenship law and the form a person would fill out. And as you can see, the date of these rules wasn't established in 1995, it was 8 January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The record -- it says: The records on citizenship have been entered in a register of citizens of the Registry office of, and in the municipality of," et cetera. And now if I could show you next document, which is 1D40-0098. Mrs. Rehn, this is a protocol between Serbia and Croatia in 2003. If you look at it, it's protocol of takeover where the government of Serbia returns to Croatia, and you can go to the next pages, for the benefit of the Court, the local registers that had been removed from Croatia in 1995 and previously. There are literally hundreds of town registers that were returned in 2003. Can we go to the next page, please. Including the town of Knin, various towns in Sector South. It gives you what years we're talking about. Were you aware at the time you were preparing your reports that Croatia had no central depository of information concerning individuals' birth records or other records necessary to establish citizenship?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: In the material that you have, I have mentioned somewhere - I can't find it now - that one of the obstacles was that they had to go to Belgrade to get their papers. It was told by some of the ministers, Susak or Jarnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And my last question for today is: Having examined I assume as part of your work as the Human Rights Rapporteur the fact that the Serbian population left, does the fact that the authorities in Serbia wound up in possession of hundreds of town registers of birth would that indicate to that you there was a certain level of organisation to the departure of the Krajina Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ELISABETH REHN
utterances.text: I don't think that I should make any kind of -- of estimates on what was the truth. I know that there have been just a demand or whatever from the Serb side from Serb leaders that you should leave, and I know that President Tudjman asked the Serb population to stay. But I have seen in so many other war zones in the world that whatever is told you that, please stay, everything is okay. People don't believe it when they are just taken by the mass psychosis that, I'm afraid something terrible will happen. So I think that both sides were not efficient enough or one side was too efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you Mrs. Rehn. I would tender, Your Honour, both of these documents into evidence and I conclude for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document ID 1D40-0082 becomes Exhibit number D686. Document ID 1D40-0098 becomes Exhibit number D687.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D686 and D687 are admitted into evidence. Mr. Misetic, you said this was your last question for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What about tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We've reached agreement that I will finish by the first session. The Cermak and Markac teams will take the second session and that will leave us the full third session for re-direct and questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is more than sufficient, Mr. President. I don't think I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so we're clear. For me, I'm not sure of the exact timing, but I will have at least one hour, if not an hour and a half. Just so the Court is aware of how much time I have planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To assist the Court, a number of matters have been dealt with already by Mr. Misetic. So our issues are narrowing to under half an hour at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that means that we stay within the one hour and a half for each session. Ms. Rehn, this is also important for you to know, I would say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because there is a fair chance that we'll conclude your testimony tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thanks God. Or you're not the God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Apart from that, it is the parties, Mrs. Rehn, who give this information. We will adjourn for the day. We will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 16th of July, 9.00, in this same courtroom. But I'd first like to instruct you, Mrs. Rehn, that you should not speak about the testimony, whether already given or still to be given. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th of July, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
